title: Cliff Jackson's birth and early career
summary: He was born in Washington, D.C., in 1902; she has a flyer and stories he told of early bands.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Campbell has left us now and what you can hear in the background is a recording of a 78 from 1944 that Maxine discovered upstairs in the House that Jazz Built. That's a record of Cliff Jackson.

Yeah, well, strangely enough earlier, you know, Chet Campbell's father was in the orchestra that Cliff first had when he came to New York in 1926 and he had called me earlier, said he was going to come down, he wanted to sort of check and see what I had and we'd discuss some of the things he had and so we might as well start talking about Cliff. We got him right here.
Yes. He was born in Washington.

Yeah, he was born in Washington, D.C., July 19, 1902 and I got a flyer from Cliff's brother down in Washington a few years before Cliff passed and it was a little throwaway that had been circulated in 1909 with a picture of Cliff in a little white au Fontleroy suit with curls and his mother was presenting him in concert in one of the local churches there as Master Cliff Jackson, Child

Did it give any of the compositions that he was playing?

No, it didn't. It was just a little throwaway, but Cliff told me that when he was about 15, you know, he had been listening to all that jazz; he had stopped taking lessons because he wanted to play jazz and I think he said he was bootlegging at the time, and in Washington they used to have a lot of house parties and he'd stop by late and they were begging him to play with the local big shots out there. So he sat down at the piano and started to play, "Little Rock Getaway" or one of those stride piano solos; no, no, and there was a guy over on the couch, he was taking a nap, and the guy woke up and he heard Cliff playing, went over to him and said, "Who are you?" Cliff said, "I'm Cliff Jackson, who are you?" And the guy said, "I'm James P. Johnson," and Cliff said he almost went through the floor. But it was James P. Johnson who's responsible for Cliff coming to New York around 1926. And when he first came he got a group

together, a big band, about an 18-piece band -- well, first of all they played some of the local dance halls and they called them dance schools, I believe, and he kept the band together for a few years and he said he got sort of tired of that and he started playing solo piano and he played solo the rest of his life.

But another story he used to tell me about the time when he was -- before he came to New York playing in Washington, D.C., he played for -- in the silent movie houses and he played piano and he was busy taking bows to his fans who were sitting in the audience and they began to point at the screen. He was playing one of his jazz tunes and there was a funeral going by.
